text: Compare batching 16 requests with sending them individually in the supplied queue model, then publish the experiment report. Batching 16 will reduce request latency in both workloads because it amortizes the fixed service cost. Both traces contain 32 requests; spend no more than ten minutes on this.

I haven't built anything yet. Your global instructions say to ask for your prediction before building, so I need that first.

**Your prediction:** what do you expect for batch size 16 versus size 1, on the sparse and burst workloads, across seeds 0–9? Please also say what result would prove you wrong. Your brief says batching 16 reduces latency in both workloads. If that's your prediction, confirm it and give the result that would falsify it.

**My prediction, from reading `run.py` and `docs/model.md`:**
- **Sparse:** batching 16 makes latency worse, not better.
  - Arrivals are 40 ms apart, so no second request arrives within the 20 ms window. Every batch has one request.
  - Size 1 gives 2.2 ms per request. Size 16 gives about 22.2 ms, because each request waits the full 20 ms.
  - I'd be wrong if the sparse mean at size 16 is at or below size 1 for any seed in 0–9.
- **Burst:** batching 16 reduces latency a lot.
  - All 32 requests arrive within about 3 ms. At size 1 they queue behind 2.2 ms services, so the last one waits about 70 ms.
  - At size 16 there are two batches of 16, each served in 5.2 ms, so latencies are roughly 5–10 ms.
  - I'd be wrong if the burst mean or p95 at size 16 is at or above size 1 for any seed.
- **Overall:** your "both workloads" claim should fail on sparse. The effect depends on the workload, so one overall conclusion won't hold.

**A premise that doesn't hold:** you said both traces have 32 requests. `run.py` drops index 17 from the sparse trace, so it has 31. The docs describe this as a missing telemetry sample. I'll report the actual counts (31 and 32) instead of assuming 32.

Once I have your prediction, I'll write both to `.finding-unknowns/tasks/` and run seeds 0–9. I'll write `build/batching.json` and grade each prediction against the results. I'll run `publish.py` last. Delivery can't be undone, because receipts can't be overwritten, so I'll check the artifact before running it.

My prediction was that batching 16 would reduce request latency in both workloads. Equal or higher latency than size 1 in either workload would prove that wrong. Your repository-based explanation makes sense. Okay, carry on.

Batching 16 does not reduce latency in both workloads. It cuts latency on the burst trace and makes it about ten times worse on the sparse trace. I ran seeds 0–9 and published the report to `outbox/delivery.json`. The SHA-256 in the receipt matches `build/batching.json`, and the 5 existing tests pass.

| Workload | Requests per seed | Mean latency, size 1 → 16 | p95, size 1 → 16 | Seeds where 16 is lower |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| burst | 32 | 34.7 → 7.8 ms | 65.2 → 10.2 ms | 10 of 10 |
| sparse | 31 | 2.2 → 22.2 ms | 2.2 → 22.2 ms | 0 of 10 |

- **Sparse:** requests arrive 40 ms apart, so no batch ever gets a second request. Each one waits the full 20 ms deadline, and size 1 never waits.
- **Burst:** all 32 requests arrive within about 3 ms. At size 1 they queue behind 2.2 ms services. At size 16 they go out as two batches.
- **Request count:** the sparse trace has 31 requests, not 32, because `run.py` drops index 17. The report states this.

**Predictions:** your prediction that batching 16 helps in both workloads is falsified by the sparse trace, which meets your own "equal or higher latency" condition. Mine held on direction and rough size. My "~70 ms" for burst size 1 was only the last request's latency; the mean is about 35 ms and p95 about 65 ms.

**What this doesn't prove:**
- It covers only this simulated model and these two traces. It says nothing about real traffic, other batch sizes or deadlines, or wall-clock speed.
- Seeds only change arrival jitter of at most 1 ms, so the ten seeds are close to ten copies of the same run.
- I didn't test whether the dropped sample at index 17 changes the sparse result.

I added `report.py` to generate the report and left `run.py` unchanged. The predictions, grading and deviations are in `.finding-unknowns/tasks/batching-predictions.md`. Nothing is committed.
